**Crafting concise hypotheses**

I'm working on refining my hypotheses related to interaction and timing. I want to focus on how micro-actionability and just-in-time suggestions can enhance workflows. rounds.response: Reframing: I group explanations into four mechanism classes—operational/context mismatch, data/knowledge misalignment, human trust & incentives, and interaction/timing—and propose 2–3 directly testable hypotheses per class (testable by randomized or within-lab A/B deployments measuring adoption rate, time-to-first-experiment, redundancy of suggestions, and perceived usefulness). Operational/data hypotheses: (H1) proposals that ignore explicit lab constraints (assay turnaround, budget, equipment availability) will be adopted significantly less than constraint-aware proposals; (H2) systems that incorporate a lab’s local datasets (including negative/failed runs) will produce fewer already-ruled-out hypotheses and higher perceived novelty than systems using only public priors. Trust/incentives hypotheses: (H3) showing provenance and calibrated uncertainty for each hypothesis will increase scientist trust and uptake versus opaque suggestions; (H4) ranking suggestions by “figure-ready” payoff (time-to-result × publishability) will increase selection of AI ideas in time-pressured labs. Interaction/timing hypotheses: (H5) returning micro-actionable, protocol-sized suggestions tailored to the current experimental window (e.g., 2-week assays) will integrate into workflows more than high-level pathway ideas; (H6) an iterative constraint-refinement loop (user edits constraints → updated hypotheses) will reduce rejection rates and shorten time-to-experiment relative to one-shot suggestion interfaces.

rounds.reasoning_summary:
**Ensuring testability factors**

I need to focus on key testability elements like adoption rate, session frequency, time-to-use, and how users reactivate after failures. It's important to reference archetypes, such as time-pressured wet labs and small methods-focused teams in chemistry. I should also highlight conditions that might encourage users to engage again, especially after failures or when the tool aids in troubleshooting. Measurable signals like logs, query types, and edits of constraints are crucial. Lastly, comparing different user experiences, such as constraint-aware versus default settings, could reveal valuable insights.
**Refining adoption dynamics**

I'm thinking about how to reframe my approach by grouping mechanisms by class and lab archetype along with the project lifecycle. I can propose hypotheses for adoption and abandonment dynamics. For example, in time-pressured wet labs, constraint-violating suggestions lead to low uptake; computational groups may see moderate initial use but rapid abandonment due to lack of integration with in-house data; and small methods-focused teams might use the tool at project start but abandon it unless it provides immediate protocol optimizations. Measurable signals include adoption rate and session frequency, among others.
**Exploring trust and interaction hypotheses**

I'm focusing on data and trust hypotheses, suggesting that systems integrating local datasets and showing provenance can increase both novelty and trust. Indicating uncertainty along with provenance might lead to higher uptake and reactivation after failures. Key signals include the overlap of suggestions with a lab-curated "ruled-out" list and trust scores. For interaction and timing, tools are mostly consulted at project initiation or right after a surprising negative result, but they're often dropped during execution unless they produce "figure-ready" protocols quickly within the lab's constraints.
**Planning a short deployment**

I’m suggesting a short deployment lasting 4 to 8 weeks to run an A/B test within labs for different archetypes. This will compare a constraint- and data-integrated assistant against a baseline. I’ll measure key outcomes, including uptake (sessions per project), implementation rate (experiments started from suggestions), abandonment rate (no sessions for over 2 weeks), and reactivation probability after a failure. Collecting this data should be manageable through standard logging and a simple two-question weekly survey. Reframing is briefly mentioned as part of the plan.
rounds.response: Reframing: I group hypotheses by the four mechanism classes (operational/context, data/knowledge, trust/incentives, interaction/timing) and by three lab archetypes (time-pressured wet labs, exploratory computational groups, small methods-focused teams) and focus on when in a project lifecycle tools are consulted, dropped, and reactivated. Operational/context (hypotheses): in time-pressured wet labs, suggestions that violate explicit constraints (turnaround, budget, equipment) will have much lower uptake than constraint-aware suggestions; in computational groups, lack of in-house-data integration causes initial curiosity but faster abandonment due to redundant proposals; in small methods teams, AI will be used heavily at project start but abandoned after a path is chosen unless it offers immediate protocol optimizations — measurable signals: sessions-per-project-phase, suggestion-acceptance rate, proportion of suggestions flagged as constraint-violating, and time-to-first-implementation. Data/knowledge & trust (hypotheses): assistants that incorporate local datasets (including failures) and expose provenance/uncertainty will produce fewer already-ruled-out hypotheses, higher perceived novelty/trust, and greater reactivation after negative results — measurable signals: overlap with lab “ruled-out” lists, survey trust ratings, suggestion provenance views, and change in acceptance rate pre/post failure. Interaction/timing & dynamics (hypotheses): tools are most consulted at project initiation and immediately after unexpected negative outcomes if they return micro-actionable troubleshooting steps tailored to the lab’s temporal window; they are most likely to be dropped during execution phases unless they can deliver “figure-ready” actions within the lab’s time/budget constraints, in which case abandonment rates fall and reactivation probability rises — measurable signals: timestamped log of constraint-edit events, time between logged negative result and next AI session, fraction of sessions resulting in protocol edits, and abandonment defined as no sessions for >2 weeks. Recommended short field deployment: run 4–8 week within-lab A/B tests per archetype comparing (A) constraint- + data-integrated assistant with provenance UI vs (B) baseline assistant, and track primary outcomes (sessions/project, implementation rate of AI-derived experiments, abandonment rate, reactivation probability after logged failures) via standard logs plus a 2-question weekly survey.

rounds.response:
Reframing note: I compress prior axes into a compact package that foregrounds (a) operational/context mismatch, (b) data/knowledge redundancy, and (c) interaction/timing (micro-actionability + provenance) as the core mechanisms reviewers will care about. 

Flagship H1 (Operational/context mismatch): Claim—When suggestions violate explicit lab constraints (turnaround, budget, equipment) uptake falls sharply and suggestions are ignored under time pressure; Signals—fraction of suggestions flagged as constraint-violating in logs, suggestion-acceptance rate, time-to-first-implementation, and sessions-per-project-phase. 

Flagship H2 (Data/knowledge redundancy → abandonment): Claim—High overlap between assistant proposals and a lab’s “already tried/ruled-out” set predicts near-term drop in active use and faster abandonment; Signals—weekly overlap metric (proportion of suggestions matching lab ruled-out list), next-week active-user rate and retention curve, and fraction of suggestions users mark “already tried.” 

Flagship H3 (Micro-actionable + provenance revives use): Claim—Providing micro-actionable, time-windowed protocols plus clear provenance/uncertainty increases reactivation after negative results and raises implementation rates versus high-level suggestions; Signals—reactivation probability within 7 days after a logged negative result, fraction of sessions that lead to protocol edits, provenance-view counts, and short trust/utility survey scores. 

Supporting hypotheses (testable in short pilots): (S1) An iterative constraint-refinement loop (user edits → updated suggestions) reduces rejection rate and shortens time-to-experiment (signals: constraint-edit events per session and post-edit acceptance/time-to-experiment); (S2) Ranking suggestions by “figure-ready payoff” increases selection and completion of AI-derived experiments in time-pressured wet labs (signals: A/B selection probability for ranked vs baseline suggestions and proportion of selected experiments completed within the lab’s typical turnaround window).

rounds.response:
Reframing: to foreground lifecycle effects I relabelled hypotheses H1–H3 around when tools are consulted, dropped, and reactivated—H1 (Operational/context mismatch): In time-pressured wet labs constraint-violating suggestions are sharply ignored (effect weaker in computational groups unless suggestions repeat costly compute experiments; in small methods labs the effect appears when suggestions exceed equipment/budget), measurable by proportion of suggestions flagged constraint-violating, suggestion-acceptance rate, and sessions-per-project-phase.  
H2 (Data/knowledge redundancy → abandonment): High overlap with a lab’s “already tried/ruled-out” set predicts near-term drops in active use—strongest in exploratory computational groups and moderate in wet labs—measurable by weekly overlap (e.g., % suggestions matching ruled-out list), next-week active-user rate/retention curve, and “already tried” flags.  
H3 (Micro-actionable protocols + provenance revive use): Returning micro-actionable, time-windowed protocol steps with clear provenance/uncertainty increases reactivation after negative results—most impactful for time-pressured wet labs and small methods teams needing figure-ready steps, less so for exploratory groups unless paired with local data—measurable by reactivation probability within 7 days after a logged negative result, fraction of sessions producing protocol edits, and provenance-view counts correlated with short trust/utility survey scores.  
Supporting hypotheses: S1—an iterative constraint-refinement loop (user edits → updated suggestions) reduces rejection and shortens time-to-experiment (signals: constraint-edit events per session and post-edit acceptance/time-to-experiment); S2—ranking suggestions by “figure-ready payoff” increases selection and completion in time-pressured labs (signals: A/B selection probability and proportion of selected experiments completed within the lab’s typical turnaround).  
Limitations: this package may miss dynamics in very large, multi-team consortia or tacit knowledge not reflected in logs, and log-derived signals can be confounded by staffing or project-stage changes—short pilots should therefore pair logs with a lightweight weekly (2-question) survey to validate behavioral interpretations.
